beginner: Parsnips need deep, loose, stone-free soil more than almost any other vegetable, because the root grows very long (often 10 to 12 inches) and straight down. Dig and loosen the bed at least 12 inches deep and pull out every rock, clod, and root, since anything the parsnip hits makes it fork or grow stubby. Light, sandy soil grows the best roots; heavy clay grows short, twisted ones, so mix in compost or use a deep raised bed. Do not add fresh manure or heavy fertilizer, which causes forking and hairy roots. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 7.0, and rake the surface fine so the slow seeds make good contact.
seasoned: Parsnip quality is set in the seedbed: the root runs long, commonly 10 to 12 inches, so the bed is worked deeply and finely. UMN recommends sandy, loamy soils and warns that shallow, heavy, or rocky ground is poor for parsnips. (UMN Extension) Loosen and remove stones and clods to at least 12 inches; any obstruction forks, kinks, or stunts the taproot. A loose sandy loam gives the straightest roots, while clay and compacted ground produce short, misshapen ones and are best improved with compost or grown in deep raised beds. Avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen, which drive forked, hairy roots, and keep pH slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0 (Clemson advises liming to about 6.0 to 6.5). Rake a fine, even, crust-free surface, since the slow seed needs close soil contact to emerge.

beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Parsnips do best from about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. Very acidic soil, below about 5.5, holds them back and worsens problems like canker, so a soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime. Clemson suggests liming to about 6.0 to 6.5 for this group of root crops.
seasoned: Parsnips grow best at a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Clemson advises liming the bed to a pH of 6.0 to 6.5 for the carrot-beet-radish-parsnip group. (Clemson HGIC) Strongly acidic soil, below about 5.5, depresses growth and is associated with more root canker, while very alkaline soil reduces micronutrient availability. A standard soil test from your local extension office removes the guesswork before sowing; lime is worked in ahead of planting since it acts slowly.

beginner: Parsnips do not need much feeding, and too much nitrogen actually hurts them, growing big leafy tops and forked, hairy roots instead of one clean root. Mix a low-nitrogen balanced fertilizer like 5-10-10 into the bed before planting, and give at most one light feeding when the plants are about 4 inches tall. Skip fresh manure, and use finished compost instead of strong fertilizer.
seasoned: Parsnips are light feeders and especially sensitive to excess nitrogen, which drives leafy tops and forked, hairy roots at the expense of a clean taproot. Clemson recommends a 5-10-10 fertilizer worked in before planting at about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet, with an optional side-dressing of a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate when plants are about 4 inches tall. (Clemson HGIC) Avoid fresh manure entirely, and lean on well-finished compost rather than concentrated nitrogen.

beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Parsnips do best with a low-nitrogen blend where the first number is smaller, like 5-10-10, mixed into the soil before planting. Do not use high-nitrogen fertilizer, which gives leafy tops and forked, hairy roots instead of good ones.
seasoned: Parsnips want steady phosphorus and potassium for root development and only modest nitrogen, so a low-first-number blend such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before sowing suits them well. Clemson gives a rate near 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet. Excess nitrogen is the classic parsnip mistake, producing lush tops and forked, hairy roots.

beginner: Mix a low-nitrogen balanced fertilizer like 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), and feed lightly just once more if the plants look weak. A little compost goes a long way.
seasoned: About 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet worked into the bed before sowing, per Clemson, plus an optional light side-dressing at the 4-inch stage. Most of the nutrition comes from incorporated compost.

beginner: Parsnips are slow and easygoing neighbors. A common trick is to sow fast radishes in the same row: they come up quickly, mark where the slow parsnips are, and are pulled long before the parsnips need the space. Onions and other alliums make tidy neighbors and their smell is widely said to help mask carrot-family root pests. The main thing to keep apart from parsnips is other carrot-family crops like carrots, celery, and dill, which share the same pests and diseases. As always, do not trust every companion chart online, since many of their claims have never been tested.
seasoned: Parsnip companions are largely traditional rather than trial-proven. The most practical pairing is interplanting fast radishes as a row marker for the slow-germinating parsnip, a long-standing technique. Alliums (onions, leeks) are commonly listed as good neighbors for root crops on space and scent-masking grounds. The clearest caution is grouping parsnip with other Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley, dill): they share carrot rust fly and soilborne problems, so they are kept apart and rotated. As University of Minnesota's review stresses, most companion claims are tradition rather than tested science, so treat them as sensible defaults and watch your own results.

beginner: Parsnip seeds are very slow, so gardeners sow quick radishes in the same row. The radishes pop up in days and show you where the row is, and you pull and eat them long before the parsnips get big. A classic trick for a slow crop.
seasoned: Sowing a few fast radishes along the parsnip row is the classic marker interplant: radishes emerge in days, flag the slow row so it is not hoed by mistake, help keep the surface from crusting, and are pulled well before the parsnips size up. A space-and-timing benefit, not a pest one.

beginner: Onions, leeks, and garlic grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck in beside parsnips without crowding them, and their strong smell is widely used to help confuse carrot-family root pests. A popular, space-saving pairing.
seasoned: Alliums are a classic interplant for carrot-family roots: shallow-rooted and upright, they share the bed without competing for the parsnip's space, and their sulfur volatiles are widely credited with masking the crop from carrot rust fly. The space benefit is solid; the pest-deterrence is plausible but not proven for parsnip specifically.

beginner: Parsnips, carrots, celery, parsley, and dill are all in the same plant family and share the same pests and diseases, especially carrot rust fly and root canker. Growing them right next to each other just helps those problems spread, so keep them apart and rotate them around the garden.
seasoned: The clearest avoid for parsnip is its own family: carrot, celery, parsley, and dill share carrot rust fly (whose larvae predispose roots to Itersonilia canker) and soilborne problems, which build up when the Apiaceae are grown together or in succession. Keep them apart in space and on a three-year rotation.

beginner: The lower part of the root gets rusty, reddish-brown tunnels and scars, sometimes with small maggots inside. Bad damage stunts the plant and lets root rot get in. Because parsnips sit in the ground for months, the damage can build up.
seasoned: Rusty, reddish-brown tunnels and surface scarring honeycomb the lower root, often with the maggots present; heavy feeding stunts plants and the wounds open the door to parsnip canker. Because parsnip is in the ground a long time, late-season damage can be significant.

beginner: The maggots of the carrot rust fly (also called carrot fly), a small fly whose young tunnel into carrot-family roots. There are usually two or more rounds a year, and the longer the roots are in the ground, the worse it gets. (USU Extension; RHS)
seasoned: The larvae of the carrot rust fly (carrot fly), a small fly whose maggots mine the roots of carrot-family crops. There are typically two or more generations a season, and damage worsens the longer roots stay in the ground. (USU Extension; RHS)

beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already tunneled, so this is about prevention. Pull and remove damaged roots, do not leave leftovers in the bed, and harvest before the late-season flies build up.
seasoned: There is no rescue for tunneled roots; management is preventive. Lift damaged roots and do not leave culls in the bed, and harvest before late-season generations build. Naturally occurring controls and good rotation reduce pressure.

beginner: Cover the bed with a fine insect mesh or row cover right after sowing to keep the flies from laying eggs. This is the best home defense. (RHS) Move parsnips away from where carrots or their relatives grew, and do not leave roots in the ground longer than you need to where this pest is bad.
seasoned: A floating row cover or fine insect mesh laid over the bed at sowing keeps the egg-laying flies off and is the most effective home defense. (RHS) Rotate parsnips away from where carrot-family crops grew, avoid leaving roots in the ground longer than needed where pressure is high, and time sowings to dodge peak fly flights.

beginner: You will see pale, squiggly trails or blotchy patches inside the leaves, where the little larvae feed between the top and bottom of the leaf. Since you eat the parsnip root, not the leaves, this is mostly a looks problem.
seasoned: Pale, winding tunnels or blotches appear inside the leaves where the larvae feed between the leaf surfaces. On parsnip, grown for the root, this is mostly cosmetic and rarely affects the harvest unless young plants are heavily mined.

beginner: The young of small leafmining flies that tunnel inside the leaves. They can have several rounds in a season. (USU Extension)
seasoned: The larvae of leafmining flies that tunnel within the foliage of carrot-family and other crops. Several generations can occur in a season. (USU Extension)

beginner: Pick off and throw away (do not compost) leaves with trails in them, which gets rid of the larvae. Sprays usually do not work because the pest is tucked inside the leaf, and healthy plants grow past light damage.
seasoned: Pick off and destroy mined leaves as they appear, which removes the larvae; sprays are largely ineffective because the larvae are protected inside the leaf. Vigorous plants outgrow light damage.

beginner: A row cover keeps the flies off, and clearing old leaves and weeds nearby cuts down the pest. Pulling off the first trailed leaves you see helps too.
seasoned: A floating row cover excludes the egg-laying flies, and clearing crop debris and weed hosts reduces carryover. Removing the first mined leaves promptly breaks the cycle.

beginner: The little hopping insect does not do much direct damage itself. The problem is that it carries the aster yellows disease from plant to plant, which makes the tops yellow, twisted, and bunched and the roots thin, hairy, and bitter (see the aster yellows entry).
seasoned: The leafhopper itself does little direct feeding damage; the concern is that it transmits aster yellows. Plants infected by way of the leafhopper show yellowed, twisted, bunchy tops and slender, hairy, bitter roots (see the aster yellows disease entry).

beginner: The aster leafhopper, a small insect that spreads the aster yellows disease as it feeds from plant to plant. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension; USU Extension)
seasoned: The aster leafhopper, a small wedge-shaped insect that moves the aster yellows phytoplasma between plants as it feeds. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension; USU Extension)

beginner: Trying to spray the leafhoppers to stop aster yellows usually does not work and is not recommended. Instead, pull out infected plants and weedy hosts right away. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
seasoned: Controlling the leafhopper to prevent aster yellows is generally not effective and not recommended; the practical response is to remove infected plants and weed reservoirs promptly. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

beginner: Pull out infected plants and weeds like dandelions that hold the disease, and a row cover can help keep the hoppers off a small bed. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
seasoned: Remove infected plants and nearby broadleaf weeds such as dandelion that harbor the phytoplasma, and a floating row cover can reduce leafhopper access to a small planting. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

beginner: Brown, black, or purple-black rotten patches form mostly on the crown and shoulders (the top) of the root, and the rot can spread until the whole root is ruined. Leaves can get small orange-brown spots with a pale halo. It is worst on roots left late in the season. (UMass)
seasoned: Reddish-brown, black, or purple-black cankers form mainly on the crown and shoulders of the root, and other microbes may follow until the whole root collapses in rot. Leaves can show small orange to brown lesions with a pale green halo. Disease is worst on late-harvested crops. (UMass)

beginner: A fungus (Itersonilia perplexans, also called black canker) that thrives in cool, wet weather. Carrot rust fly maggots make it worse by wounding the roots, and root tops sticking out of the soil let it in. (UMass)
seasoned: The fungus Itersonilia perplexans, also called black canker, favored by cool, wet weather. Carrot rust fly larvae predispose roots to infection by wounding them, and exposed shoulders are an entry point. (UMass)

beginner: There is no cure once a root has it, and sprays do not work on root canker. Dig and use the good roots and throw out the rotten ones. The fix is in how you grow the next crop. (UMass)
seasoned: There is no cure for infected roots, and fungicide sprays do not control root cankers. Lift and use sound roots, and discard rotted ones; management is preventive and cultural. (UMass)

beginner: Grow a canker-resistant variety, do not plant parsnips or their relatives in the same bed for two to three years, mound a little soil over the root shoulders during the season, keep carrot rust fly down, avoid soggy soil, and clear and bury old parsnip plants after harvest. (UMass)
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties (Avonresister, Cobham Improved Marrow), rotate out of the carrot family for two to three years, hill soil over the shoulders through the season, control carrot rust fly, avoid waterlogged beds, harvest before very late in cold wet spells, and bury old parsnip residue by deep cultivation to lower inoculum. (UMass)

beginner: Infected plants get yellow or reddish, twisted, bunched-up tops, and the root stays thin and grows a beard of fine hairy roots, often tasting bitter. There is no cure. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
seasoned: Infected plants show yellowed, reddened, twisted, and bunchy tops, and the taproot stays slender and grows a mass of fine hairy rootlets; affected roots often taste bitter. There is no cure. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

beginner: A bacteria-like organism (a phytoplasma) carried from plant to plant by the aster leafhopper. It also lives in many weeds and flowers, which act as a source. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
seasoned: The aster yellows phytoplasma, a bacterium-like organism that lives in the plant's phloem and is spread plant to plant by the aster leafhopper. It also infects many weeds and ornamentals that serve as reservoirs. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

beginner: There is no cure. Pull out any plant you think is infected, plus weeds like dandelions, to slow the spread. Spraying the insect that carries it usually does not help. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
seasoned: There is no cure. Remove plants suspected of infection promptly, including weed hosts such as dandelion, to limit spread; trying to control the leafhopper vector is generally ineffective. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

beginner: Keep weeds down, pull infected plants right away, and use a row cover on a small bed to keep the leafhoppers off. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
seasoned: Keep down broadleaf weeds that host the phytoplasma, remove infected plants as soon as they are spotted, and use a floating row cover on small plantings to reduce leafhopper access. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or tiny seedlings that flop over and die with a dark, pinched, wet-looking spot at the base of the stem. You see it as bare gaps in the row. Because parsnips are so slow to sprout, they are exposed to this for a long time.
seasoned: Seeds fail to emerge, or the slow young seedlings topple and collapse with a dark, water-soaked, pinched spot at the stem base. Losses show as bare gaps in the row. Parsnip's long germination prolongs the vulnerable window the pathogens exploit.

beginner: Soil organisms (mostly Pythium and Rhizoctonia) that attack sprouting seeds and baby seedlings, worst in cool, soggy, poorly drained soil and when you overwater. Old seed and a hard, wet seedbed make it worse.
seasoned: Soilborne pathogens, chiefly Pythium and Rhizoctonia species, favored by cool, wet, poorly drained soil and overwatering. Old or weak seed and a crusted, slow-draining seedbed increase losses.

beginner: Seedlings that have flopped will not recover. If it shows up, stop watering for a bit to let the surface dry, and clear away the fallen seedlings. There is no good home cure, so this one is about prevention.
seasoned: Affected seedlings cannot be saved. If it appears, stop watering and let the surface dry somewhat, and clear collapsed seedlings; there is no home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is the lever.

beginner: Use fresh seed, wait until the soil is warm enough (about 50°F) and not cold and soggy, keep the seedbed damp but not soaking, do not plant too deep, and improve drainage or use a raised bed on heavy soil.
seasoned: Sow fresh seed into warm-enough (about 50°F), well-drained soil rather than cold, wet ground, keep the seedbed evenly moist without saturating it, do not sow too deep, and improve drainage or use raised beds on heavy soil.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, and pay closest attention while the slow seeds are sprouting and later while the roots are bulking up. From planting until the sprouts appear (often 2 to 3 weeks), keep the surface moist so it does not dry into a hard crust. After that, give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain.
seasoned: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most during the long, slow germination window and again as the roots size up. From sowing until the seedlings are up, often 2 to 3 weeks, the surface must stay moist and uncrusted. Once established, parsnips want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain.

beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, including rain, once the plants are growing. While the seeds are sprouting, just keep the top of the soil damp, not soggy.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week including rainfall once established, adjusted up in heat or sandy soil. During germination the seedbed needs only enough to stay evenly moist near the surface, not soaked. (UMN Extension)

beginner: Water gently at soil level, using a soft spray, soaker hose, or drip line. A hard blast from the hose can wash out the shallow seeds or pack the soil into a crust the slow sprouts cannot push through.
seasoned: Water at the base with a gentle setting, soaker hose, or drip line to keep the surface evenly moist without crusting the bed or washing out the shallow-sown seed.

beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, parsnips can rot and seedlings can damp off. Watch for yellow leaves, soft roots, and a constantly wet, sour-smelling bed. If you see these, water less and make sure the soil drains well.
seasoned: Constantly saturated soil invites damping-off and root rots and can worsen canker; yellowing tops, soft roots, and a sour, waterlogged bed are signs to back off. Poor drainage is the usual cause, which is why deep, loose, well-draining soil matters.

beginner: Dry, cracked soil on top, droopy or dull leaves, and slow growth mean the parsnips need more water. Letting them go bone dry and then soaking them cracks the roots, so keep the watering steady.
seasoned: Dry, cracked surface soil, dull or wilting tops, and slow growth signal too little water. A dry spell followed by heavy watering makes the roots take up water fast and split, the most common parsnip watering fault.

beginner: Parsnip seeds are slow, taking 2 to 3 weeks to come up, and they will not survive drying out even once. Keep the top of the soil damp every day until the little seedlings appear.
seasoned: Parsnip germination is long and notoriously erratic, often 2 to 3 weeks, and a single dry-out kills the fragile emerging seedlings. Keep the surface continuously moist and uncrusted the entire time; many gardeners cover the row or water daily until the stand is up.

beginner: After the seedlings are up, water a bit less often but keep the soil evenly damp so the long root grows straight.
seasoned: Once up, ease into steady, even moisture that encourages the long taproot to grow straight and down.

beginner: As the roots grow over the long season, give a steady soak of about 1 inch a week. Big swings between dry and wet crack the roots.
seasoned: Root sizing is the second critical window over this long season. Keep growth even at about an inch a week in deeper soakings; uneven watering is what cracks the roots. Adjust up in heat or sandy soil.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while the roots grow. You can leave parsnips in the ground into winter, where frost makes them sweeter, and they need little water once it is cold.
seasoned: Hold even moisture through sizing. Parsnips can stay in the ground into winter and sweeten after frost, needing little water once cool weather sets in.

beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, water gently so you do not wash them out or make a hard crust. Once the parsnips are up and growing, water more deeply but less often. Sudden swings from dry to soaked are what crack the roots.
seasoned: On a fresh seedbed, keep the surface evenly moist without crusting or dislodging the shallow seed, using a fine setting, soaker hose, or drip. After establishment, shift to deeper, less frequent soakings to keep roots growing steadily and prevent the dry-then-wet swings that crack them.

seasoned: Two windows matter most. The first is the long germination through emergence, when the surface must stay continuously moist and uncrusted or the stand fails. The second is the root-sizing period, when steady moisture keeps growth even and prevents the cracking that follows uneven watering.

beginner: You do not need to harden off parsnips. They are sown straight into the garden from seed, not started indoors and transplanted.

Plant parsnip seeds right in the garden where they will grow, not in pots, because the long root does not move well. The most important thing is to use fresh seed every single year: parsnip seed goes bad fast, and old seed is the number one reason parsnips fail to come up. Sow the seed about 1/2 inch deep once the soil has warmed to about 50°F, and keep the surface damp. Be very patient, because the seeds are slow, often 2 to 3 weeks and sometimes longer. A handy trick is to scatter a few fast radish seeds in the same row to mark where the parsnips are.
seasoned: Always direct-sow parsnips; they have a long taproot and resent transplanting, which forks and stunts the root. The single most important rule is fresh seed: parsnip seed does not store well and loses viability within a year, so buy new seed every season. (Clemson HGIC; RHS) Sow about 1/2 inch deep once the soil is workable and at least 50°F, keeping the surface evenly moist, because germination is slow and erratic, often 2 to 3 weeks and sometimes far longer. (UMN Extension; Clemson HGIC) Many growers mix in a few fast radish seeds to mark the slow row and break any crust. There is no indoor-start or hardening-off step.

beginner: For parsnips, the pot needs to be deep, because the root grows very long (10 to 12 inches). Give them at least 15 inches of soil depth; a shallow pot makes short, forked roots. Choose a short, stubby parsnip variety for containers, since the long kinds are hard to grow in pots. Use a tall grow bag or deep tub with drainage holes, and remember the pot is in use for months, since parsnips are slow.
seasoned: Depth is the governing constraint. Parsnip roots commonly reach 10 to 12 inches, so a container must be deeper than the root, ideally 15 inches or more of loose soil; shallow pots produce stunted, forked roots. (UMN Extension) Short, stump-rooted cultivars are the realistic container choice; long types are impractical in pots. A tall, wide grow bag or deep tub with drainage holes works; the long season means the pot is occupied for months.

beginner: Pick a parsnip variety to match your soil and your disease pressure. Long old kinds like Hollow Crown need deep, loose soil to grow well; shorter kinds (like Lancer or Avonresister) handle shallower or heavier soil and pots better. If root canker (a brown rot on the shoulders) is a problem where you garden, choose a canker-resistant variety such as Avonresister, Cobham Improved Marrow, Gladiator, or Javelin. Harris Model and All American are good dependable choices. Whatever you grow, buy fresh seed every year, because parsnip seed does not keep.
seasoned: Parsnip variety choice turns on root length versus your soil depth and on canker resistance. Long heirlooms like Hollow Crown need deep, stone-free soil to size up, while shorter modern types (Lancer, Avonresister) suit shallower or heavier ground and containers. Where Itersonilia canker recurs, choose a resistant or tolerant cultivar (Avonresister, Cobham Improved Marrow, Gladiator, Javelin). (RHS) Harris Model and All American are reliable all-rounders. Most parsnips mature in about 100 to 120 days and all need fresh seed each year.

beginner: Do not grow parsnips where you grew parsnips, carrots, celery, parsley, or dill last year. These are all in the same plant family and share the same pests (carrot rust fly) and root diseases (canker), which build up in the soil over time. Also avoid beds that got a lot of manure for the last crop, since leftover nitrogen makes parsnips fork and grow hairy. Wait about three years before parsnips or their relatives go back into the same bed.
seasoned: Do not plant parsnips where another carrot-family crop (Apiaceae) grew the previous season, including parsnip, carrot, celery, parsley, dill, or fennel, since they share carrot rust fly and soilborne diseases such as Itersonilia canker that build up where the family is grown repeatedly. Avoid beds heavily manured for the previous crop, because residual nitrogen drives forking and hairy roots. The standard guideline is a three-year gap before parsnips or their relatives return to a bed; deep cultivation that buries old parsnip residue also lowers canker inoculum.

beginner: Move your parsnips to a different spot each year, and do not put them (or relatives like carrots, celery, and dill) back in the same bed for about three years. This keeps shared pests and the root canker disease from piling up. Parsnips do well following beans or peas, which add nitrogen, or following leafy greens.
seasoned: Rotate parsnips on a three-year cycle, keeping them and all other carrot-family crops out of a bed for two to three seasons after they are grown there. This breaks the buildup of carrot rust fly and the soilborne fungus behind Itersonilia canker, which is worse where parsnip residue and the family persist. (UMass) Following a legume or a light feeder suits parsnips; following a heavily manured crop does not, because residual nitrogen causes forking.

beginner: Parsnips are a long-season, cool-weather root vegetable in the carrot family. The part you eat is one long, sweet, cream-colored root. Always plant the seeds right where they will grow, and use fresh seed every single year, because parsnip seed goes bad fast and old seed is the main reason parsnips fail. Be patient: the seeds are very slow, often 2 to 3 weeks or more to come up, and they will not break through a dry crust, so keep the surface damp. Parsnips need deep, loose, rock-free soil for their long root (often 8 to 12 inches) and take a long time, about 100 to 120 days. They are a biennial, which means if you leave them past their first winter they shoot up a flower and the root turns woody, so dig overwintered ones before spring. The best thing about parsnips is that frost makes them sweet: the cold turns starch into sugar, so you harvest them after frost and can leave them in the ground all winter, digging them as you need them, sweeter every week. In hot-summer areas, grow them in fall for a winter harvest. One safety note: the leaves and juice can give some people a skin rash in sunlight, so wear gloves on sunny days.
seasoned: Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) is a long-season, cool-climate root crop in the carrot family, grown for its sweet, ivory taproot. It is direct-sown only, and the single most important rule is fresh seed: parsnip seed loses viability within a year, so old seed is the leading cause of failure. Germination is notoriously slow and erratic, often 2 to 3 weeks and sometimes far longer, and the fine seedlings cannot push through a crusted surface, so the seedbed must stay evenly moist for weeks. The crop needs deep, loose, stone-free soil for its long root (commonly 8 to 12 inches) and grows for roughly 100 to 120 days, longer for a late crop. Parsnip is a biennial grown as an annual for the root: it stores energy the first year and bolts to flower the second, so overwintered roots are dug before spring regrowth. Its defining trait is cold-sweetening: frost converts root starch to sugar, so parsnips are harvested after hard frost and are famously left in the ground over winter, dug as needed and growing sweeter the longer they wait. Where summers are hot, parsnip is a fall-sown, winter-harvested crop. One handling note: the foliage and sap can cause a skin rash in sunlight, so gloves are worn when working among the plants on bright days.

beginner: Parsnips are ready when the roots are full sized, often 1 1/2 to 2 inches across at the top and 8 to 12 inches long, with the leafy tops dying down in fall, usually about 100 to 120 days after planting. But the real signal is cold weather, not a date: parsnips get much sweeter after a few frosts, as the cold turns starch into sugar, so there is no rush. They keep right in the ground, and in cold areas you can pile straw over the row and dig them through winter and into early spring, and they taste sweeter the longer they wait. Loosen the soil next to the row with a garden fork before pulling, because the long roots break easily. Dig any you left in over winter before they start growing again in spring, or the root turns woody. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the leaves on a sunny day, since the sap can give some people a rash.

beginner: With parsnips, getting the bed right before you plant matters more than almost anything else, because the root grows very long (8 to 12 inches) and anything it hits makes it fork or come out stubby. Dig and loosen the soil at least 12 inches down and pull out rocks, hard clumps, and roots. Loose, sandy soil grows the straightest parsnips; heavy clay grows short, twisted ones, so mix in compost or use a deep raised bed. Do not add fresh manure or a lot of high-nitrogen fertilizer, which grows leafy tops and forked, hairy roots; use finished compost and a low-nitrogen blend like 5-10-10. Rake the top smooth and fine so the small, slow seeds sit snug against the soil, and aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 7.0, adding lime ahead of time only if a soil test says so.
seasoned: Parsnip quality is set in the seedbed more than anywhere else, because the root runs long, commonly 8 to 12 inches, and any obstruction forks or stunts it. Work the bed deep and fine, loosening and removing stones, clods, and debris to at least 12 inches. A loose sandy loam gives the straightest, longest roots; heavy clay and compacted ground produce short, forked roots and are best improved with compost or worked into deep raised beds. Avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen, which drive forked, hairy roots and lush tops at the expense of the root; use only well-finished compost and a low-nitrogen balanced feeding such as 5-10-10. Rake the surface smooth and fine, since the small, slow seeds need close contact and an even, crust-free surface to emerge over their long germination. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH, about 6.0 to 7.0, liming ahead of sowing if a soil test calls for it.
